who: A grown son who works away from home and has come back for the harvest.
place: A two-room farmhouse at dusk, the roof leaking after a week of rain, harvest wheat still standing wet in the field.
present: his aging father, who says nothing but favors his bad hip
his younger brother's family, whose barn roof caved in yesterday
a hired hand waiting for orders
the wheat still lying in the field

factors.fact: The father raised him alone after the mother died and has never once asked him for anything.
The brother's family has no dry place to sleep tonight with the barn roof down.
The wheat will rot if it is not brought in before the next rain, likely tomorrow night.
He has one day of daylight and one hired hand to help him.
He told his brother last spring that he would always come first if trouble hit.
The father has said, more than once, that a man who worries over other men's roofs neglects his own kin.

could_also.verb: stays to bring in the wheat
splits the day between both
sends the hired hand to the brother instead

would_not.verb: tells his father to manage alone
would_not.why: He owes the man too much to say it to his face.

would_not.verb: ignores the brother's roof entirely
would_not.why: The promise from last spring is not the sort he breaks.

then: He walks the hired hand through the wheat first, telling him what must be cut by evening, then takes what tools he can carry to his brother's yard by midday. He does not tell his father which one he chose.
why: The wheat can wait one more day if the weather holds, but a family sleeping under a broken roof cannot. The promise from last spring settles it, though the father's old complaint about neglecting his own kin will not be answered.
turns_on: whether the weather will hold long enough for the wheat to wait

who: A hen with a late brood of six chicks, all still too young to fly.
place: A low bank beside a creek that has been rising all afternoon after rain in the hills.
present: the six chicks, spread along the bank
a weak seventh chick that trails behind and cannot keep up
a stand of higher ground a short run away
a dog barking somewhere across the field

factors.fact: The water is rising fast enough that the low bank will be under water within minutes.
She can only shepherd the chicks that keep pace with her.
The weak chick is hers as much as the others, and she has fussed over it since it hatched.
The higher ground is close enough that the five fast chicks can still be driven there in time.
Hens do not carry chicks; she can only call and peck them forward.
Waiting for the slow chick to catch up costs the whole brood the minutes they need.

does.verb: drives the five toward higher ground

could_also.verb: circles back for the slow chick
stands calling from the bank

would_not.verb: abandons all six and flees alone
would_not.why: The pull to the brood does not leave her even when she cannot save all of it.

would_not.verb: waits on the bank until the water reaches her
would_not.why: Waiting there drowns five chicks along with one.

then: She gets the five up the bank as the water reaches the low ground. She calls back toward the weak chick until it is out of sight, then does not return.
why: She cannot carry the slow chick and cannot wait without losing the rest. The five that can keep pace are the ones her driving can still save; the seventh is already past what her calling can do.
turns_on: whether the weak chick can be driven fast enough to keep up

who: A bridge-toll keeper who has held the same post for many years.
place: A narrow toll bridge on a cold night, the river running high and loud below.
present: a travel-worn stranger carrying a limp, feverish child
the toll box, nearly empty this late in the season
the bridge owner's standing order nailed to the post: no crossing without payment
no one else on the road at this hour

factors.fact: The keeper answers to a bridge owner who checks the toll box and dismisses keepers who let people cross free.
The child is fevered and the nearest healer is a house across the bridge, not behind.
The keeper's own wages depend on the toll box balancing at the season's end.
He has seen a child die of fever before and knows how fast it can go.
He knows a back path around the toll gate that the owner does not watch closely.
Keepers before him have been let go for smaller mercies than this.

could_also.verb: points them to the back path
pays the toll from his own pocket

would_not.verb: turns them away for lack of payment
would_not.why: The fever will not wait for the stranger to find coin.

would_not.verb: reports the crossing honestly in the toll ledger
would_not.why: An honest entry invites the exact question he cannot afford to answer.

then: He lets them through and marks the ledger as if no one crossed that night. He lies awake wondering if the owner will notice the missing entry at the season's count.
why: A child's fever outweighs a night's toll, and the healer is only reachable by crossing. The risk to his own post is real, but not one he can weigh evenly against a dying child in front of him.
turns_on: whether the bridge owner checks the ledger closely enough to notice

who: A night watchman guarding a merchant's grain store.
place: A locked grain store at the end of a hungry winter, the town's own stores long empty.
present: sacks of grain stacked to the roof
his own family at home, who have eaten little in two days
the merchant who pays his wage and trusts him with the only key
a hungry stray dog scratching at the door

factors.fact: His children have had nothing but broth for two days.
The merchant pays him precisely to see that no grain leaves this store without a ledger entry.
Being caught taking grain means losing the post and the wage his family depends on entirely.
He holds the only key and no one would know if a small amount went missing.
A watchman who steals from the store he guards is, by long custom, never trusted with a key again anywhere in the district.

could_also.verb: takes a small handful for his children
asks the merchant directly for an advance

would_not.verb: lets the stray dog break in and take the blame
would_not.why: It would not feed his children and would still be a theft he arranged.

would_not.verb: takes a full sack
would_not.why: That much is missed by morning and ends the post for certain.

then: He finishes the watch with the grain untouched and walks home at dawn to ask the merchant, in daylight, for an advance against next month's wage.
why: The wage from this post feeds his family for months; a night's theft feeds them for a day and risks all of it. The hunger is real, but asking outright costs him less than taking outright.
turns_on: whether the merchant would grant an advance if asked plainly

who: A ground-nesting bird with a clutch of nearly-fledged young.
place: A hedgerow at the edge of a field in early evening, a fox working its way along the same hedge.
present: the four young, crouched low in the nest and not yet able to fly far
a fox moving closer along the hedge line, testing the ground for prey
open field with no cover on either side
the bird's own exposed position a few feet from the nest

factors.fact: The fox is close enough to reach the nest within a minute if nothing distracts it.
A fox that catches an adult bird kills it outright; there is no bargaining with it.
The young are close to fledging and have survived this far only because she has not left them exposed before.
Dragging a wing and calling loudly can pull a fox's attention away from a nest toward open ground.
The trick only works if the fox has not already fixed on the nest's scent.

does.verb: drags a wing and draws off

could_also.verb: freezes low and silent over the nest
flies off and abandons the nest

would_not.verb: attacks the fox directly
would_not.why: A bird her size cannot fight a fox and win.

would_not.verb: stays sitting on the nest and hopes it passes
would_not.why: A fox that finds the nest occupied kills the sitting bird along with the young.

then: She flutters into the open field calling and trailing a wing, drawing the fox thirty yards off before breaking away and flying clear. She circles back to the nest once the fox has moved on.
why: Fighting the fox outright is not a fight she can win, and freezing risks the fox finding the nest by scent regardless. Drawing it off costs her a real risk to herself but gives the young their only real chance.
turns_on: whether the fox has already caught the nest's scent

who: A young field hand who saw a friend break a tool while using it without permission.
place: A farmyard at midday, the farm owner holding the broken plow blade and asking who is responsible.
present: the farm owner, angry over the cost of the blade
the friend, standing silent and pale nearby
two other hands who did not see what happened
the broken blade itself, showing signs of being forced past its limit

factors.fact: He saw exactly how it happened and knows his friend is at fault.
The friend has covered for him before and has a sick mother depending on this wage.
The owner has fired hands outright for breaking tools through carelessness.
The owner has been fair to him personally and has never once accused him unjustly.
Claiming the blade broke on its own is a story the owner might not believe if pressed.

does.how: that the blade simply gave out from wear

could_also.verb: tells the owner plainly what happened
says nothing and lets the silence sit

would_not.verb: blames one of the other two hands
would_not.why: That would trade one innocent person's trouble for another's.

would_not.verb: admits to breaking it himself
would_not.why: A lie that shifts blame onto himself still is not the truth the owner is owed.

then: The owner grumbles about worn tools and sends them back to work. Afterward the friend thanks him quietly and neither of them mentions it again.
why: The friend's mother and wage weigh more than the owner's fairness in this one moment, even though the lie sits badly with him. It turns on whether the owner presses hard enough to catch the story falling apart.
turns_on: whether the owner presses the story hard enough to catch it

who: A gate guard under orders to turn away all refugees from a town under quarantine.
place: A town gate at dusk, a line of turned-away travelers already camped outside in the cold.
present: a pregnant woman near her time, refused entry along with the rest
the captain of the guard, who checks the gate log each night
the quarantine order, posted and signed by the town council
other guards at the gate watching how he handles it

factors.fact: The captain has flogged a guard before for letting anyone through against the order.
The woman is close enough to labor that she may not survive it in the open cold.
The quarantine exists because a fever has already killed several in the town, and one exception could open the gate to more.
The town itself is not his; he took this post for pay, not out of loyalty to it.
There is a midwife's house just inside the wall, close enough to reach quickly.

could_also.verb: turns her away with the rest
sends for the midwife to come out to her instead

would_not.verb: lets the whole line through
would_not.why: That would risk exactly the spread the order exists to stop.

would_not.verb: reports the exception to the captain openly
would_not.why: An open report invites a flogging and does nothing further for the woman.

then: He waves her through alone in the dark, walks her to the midwife's door, then returns to his post and says nothing of it in the log.
why: One woman close to labor is not the general risk the order was written against, and the fever's danger comes from crowds, not from a single quiet exception. The pay that bought his loyalty to the post does not stretch to watching her labor in the cold.
turns_on: whether one quiet exception draws the same risk as opening the gate outright

who: A working sheepdog raised from a pup by one shepherd who has since grown too old and ill to work the hills.
place: A hill farm in late autumn, the old shepherd now bedridden and a younger hired shepherd taking the flock out each day.
present: the old shepherd, calling weakly from the cottage window
the younger shepherd, whistling from the gate for the dog to come work
the flock, already moving toward the far pasture
the old shepherd's worn crook, left leaning by the door

factors.fact: The old shepherd raised the dog from a pup and trained every command it knows.
A working dog is bred to answer the whistle that calls it to the flock.
The flock needs moving today whether or not the old shepherd can walk out to do it.
The younger shepherd feeds it, works it, and is, in practice, the one it now serves each day.
The old shepherd, weak as he is, still needs the dog to lie by him through the long afternoons.

could_also.verb: stays by the old shepherd's bed
runs between the two all day
could_also.toward: the old shepherd and the younger shepherd

would_not.verb: ignores the whistle entirely
would_not.why: The training to answer that whistle runs deeper than any single day's choosing.

would_not.verb: refuses to leave the cottage even briefly
would_not.why: The flock still needs working and idle sheep are its own danger.

then: It runs to the gate at the whistle and works the flock all morning, then trots back to the cottage on its own once the sheep are settled and lies by the old shepherd's bed through the afternoon.
why: The whistle and the day's work are what the dog knows how to answer without thinking, and the flock's needs do not wait. The old bond still pulls it back once the working part of the day is done.
turns_on: whether the flock's work is finished before the day is out

who: A lean stray dog that has been living under a collapsed shed since her litter was born.
place: A market alley at dusk, cold rain starting, the shed with the puppies a few streets away.
present: a stranger crouched by a doorway with meat scraps and a blanket
the four puppies, out of sight under the shed
other stray dogs competing for scraps nearby
the rain picking up

factors.fact: She has not eaten a full meal in two days and is thin enough that her milk is drying up.
The four puppies are blind and cannot yet move to follow her.
The stranger's hand is open and still, the way a hand is when it means no harm.
The rain is turning cold enough to kill puppies that get wet and cannot dry off.
She can carry one piece of meat back in her mouth but not the warmth of a fire.
The shed is close enough to reach before the rain gets much worse.

does.verb: takes the food and carries it back

could_also.verb: stays and lets the stranger pet her
eats the food on the spot

would_not.verb: follows the stranger home
would_not.why: The puppies cannot come with her and cannot be left overnight.

would_not.verb: ignores the offered food
would_not.why: Her hunger and the milk it costs the litter are past ignoring.

then: She snatches the meat and trots back toward the shed with it in her mouth, checking behind her once. The stranger does not follow.
why: The offer is real but it does not reach the puppies, and the milk they need depends on her eating something tonight. Carrying food back costs her the fire and the safety the stranger offered, but leaves the litter no worse than it already is.
turns_on: whether the shed is close enough to reach before the rain worsens

who: A tenant farmhand who has been asked by his landlord to report which neighbor has been poaching rabbits from the estate woods.
place: The landlord's yard at midday, the estate steward waiting with a ledger.
present: the steward waiting for an answer
the neighbor's family, who the farmhand knows to be starving since the neighbor's ox died
a coil of snare wire found near the trees, evidence he could hand over
his own family's tenancy, which depends on staying in the landlord's favor

factors.fact: The steward has power to evict any tenant who is seen protecting a poacher.
The neighbor has lent him tools and helped bring in his harvest for ten years.
Naming no one keeps the neighbor's family fed through the winter.
The landlord has never once cheated him and expects the same in return.
Naming the neighbor ends the friendship for good; naming no one risks his own family's tenancy if the truth comes out later.
He knows exactly who set the snares and could say so with certainty.

could_also.verb: names the neighbor
lies and names someone else

would_not.verb: hands over the snare wire
would_not.why: It would be the same as naming the man who lent it to him.

would_not.verb: tells the neighbor to stop outright
would_not.why: Warning him risks word getting back that he knew and hid it.

then: He tells the steward he saw nothing worth reporting and hands back the coil of wire as something he found and does not recognize. He avoids the neighbor's house for a week afterward.
why: Naming the neighbor buys nothing but guilt and a broken friendship over ten years of help; staying silent risks his own tenancy if the truth surfaces later. Neither choice is bearable, so he gives the steward as little as he can without lying outright.
turns_on: whether the steward already suspects who it is

who: A young laborer who has been saving coin toward buying his own small plot of land.
place: A tavern on payday evening, a dice game going on in the corner.
present: a group of other laborers already deep in a winning streak at dice
the small pouch of saved coin, more than he has ever carried at once
the landholder's asking price, still just out of reach
his own tired reflection in the tavern's one clouded mirror

factors.fact: The land price will only be reachable after two more years of saving as things stand.
The dice game is running hot tonight and the others are goading him to sit in.
He has lost at dice before and knows exactly how it ends most nights.
The thought of two more years of the same work sits heavier on him than usual tonight.
He knows, sober and clear-eyed, that the odds do not favor him.

could_also.verb: walks home with the coin untouched
bets only a small, safe portion

would_not.verb: bets the coin and tells himself it is a sure thing
would_not.why: He already knows better than that and does not fool himself about it.

would_not.verb: lends the coin to a friend instead
would_not.why: The pull tonight is toward the game, not toward generosity.

then: He loses most of the pouch within the hour and walks home with far less than he sat down with, muttering to himself the whole way about the two years he has just added back on.
why: Two more years of the same grinding work feels unbearable tonight in a way it usually does not, and the game offers a shortcut he knows is false even as he takes it. He does it anyway, and knows exactly what it costs before he sits down.
turns_on: how unbearable two more years of saving feels tonight specifically

who: A blacksmith's apprentice, the older of two brothers left on their own since their parents died.
place: A small forge at the back of a rented room, the younger brother sick in bed nearby.
present: the younger brother, fevered and coughing badly
the forge's cracked bellows, needed to finish a paying commission due tomorrow
the last of their savings, just enough for medicine or a replacement bellows part, not both
the customer who commissioned the work and expects it on time

factors.fact: The younger brother's fever has worsened since yesterday and the apothecary's tonic could break it.
Without a working bellows, the commission cannot be finished and the customer will not pay at all.
Losing this customer's payment means no money at all next week, tonic or not.
The younger brother is the only family the apprentice has left.
The commission is due tomorrow and the part cannot be fetched and fitted same-day as buying tonic.

could_also.verb: buys the bellows part instead
tries to borrow against next week's pay

would_not.verb: lets the fever run its course untreated
would_not.why: The fever is bad enough now that waiting risks more than the money does.

would_not.verb: sells the forge's remaining good tools for both
would_not.why: That would cost him the means to earn anything at all afterward.

then: He buys the tonic and sits up with his brother through the night. In the morning he goes to the customer and asks, plainly, for a few more days to finish the work.
why: A brother's fever getting worse tonight outweighs a commission that can still be finished late, even if late risks the customer's goodwill. The tonic cannot wait; the bellows, awkwardly, still can.
turns_on: whether the customer will accept the work finished a few days late

who: A village healer who keeps a small store of fever-bark tea.
place: A one-room clinic at night during a fever going through the village.
present: a farmer's young daughter, burning hot and barely conscious
an old widow who nursed half the village through the last fever and is now sick herself
the widow's grown son, waiting outside
the last of the fever-bark, enough for one full dose

factors.fact: The child's fever is higher and her body is smaller, so the bark could break it fastest in her.
The widow spent thirty years nursing this village without asking payment.
There is enough bark for one full dose, or two weak half-doses that might not break either fever.
The healer has no standing to be told who lives, only to use what she has as best she can.
Splitting the dose could mean neither of them recovers.
The widow is old and has weathered fevers before; the child has not.

could_also.verb: splits the dose between both
gives the full dose to the widow

would_not.verb: tells the widow's son there is nothing left
would_not.why: There is a dose, and lying about it would only be to avoid the harder truth.

would_not.verb: waits for someone else to decide
would_not.why: The fever will not wait for a decision made by committee.

then: She brews the whole dose for the child and sits with her until the fever breaks toward morning. She goes to the widow's son afterward and tells him plainly there was only enough for one.
why: A split dose risks losing both; a whole dose gives one of them a real chance. The child's smaller body and higher fever make the odds better spent there, whatever is owed to the widow for years of care.
turns_on: whether splitting the dose could still break both fevers

who: An old nanny goat at the back of a small herd being driven down a mountain path ahead of an early snowstorm.
place: A narrow ridge trail an hour before dark, snow already starting.
present: the rest of the herd, moving quickly ahead down the trail
a lame kid that fell behind and can barely put weight on one leg
the herder driving from the rear
wolves that have been shadowing the herd for two days

factors.fact: The lame kid was born to another goat that died last spring, and this nanny has minded it since.
Wolves following the herd take stragglers first when the light goes.
Staying back with the kid means falling behind the safety of the herd's numbers.
Dark and the storm are close enough that the herd cannot afford to slow down.
The herder's own choice is to keep pace with the healthy animals and leave slow ones to catch up as they can.
A lone animal on the trail after dark is far more likely to be taken than one in the group.

could_also.verb: pushes ahead with the herd
nudges the kid forward relentlessly

would_not.verb: abandons the kid at the first sign of wolves
would_not.why: The bond from raising it holds even against the risk.

would_not.verb: charges the wolves
would_not.why: A goat facing down wolves alone does not save either of them.

then: She stays a length behind the herd, matching the kid's slow pace and glancing back at the tree line. The gap to the herd widens as the light fails.
why: The bond to the kid she has raised outweighs the safety of the group, at least for now, though every minute behind the herd raises the risk from the wolves. It turns on how much longer the trail is before the herd would notice and slow for them.
turns_on: how far behind the safety of the herd's numbers they fall

who: A traveling cloth merchant who has just been offered a large, fast sale by a new buyer passing through.
place: A market stall on the last day of a trading fair, wagons already being loaded to leave.
present: the new buyer, offering to take the whole remaining stock now at a good price
an old trading partner from a smaller town, arriving late and expecting the stock set aside as promised months ago
the merchant's own family waiting on the season's earnings
the fair closing within the hour

factors.fact: The merchant promised the smaller-town partner first pick of the stock back in spring, in writing.
The new buyer's price is better than the smaller-town partner has ever paid.
The smaller-town partner has bought from the merchant every year for a decade and never once been late on payment.
The new buyer is leaving within the hour and will not wait or return.
The season's earnings decide whether the merchant's family eats well or poorly through winter.
Word of a broken promise travels fast among the small-town traders the merchant depends on.

does.verb: honors the promise and sells to

could_also.verb: sells the whole stock to the new buyer
splits the stock between both buyers
could_also.toward: the new buyer and the smaller-town partner

would_not.verb: tells the smaller-town partner the stock is already gone
would_not.why: It would be a lie the partner could easily uncover before the fair closes.

would_not.verb: delays deciding until the new buyer leaves
would_not.why: The new buyer's offer expires with the hour, forcing an answer either way.

then: The merchant sells the promised portion to the smaller-town partner at the old price, then offers what remains to the new buyer, who takes it but grumbles at the smaller amount.
why: The written promise and a decade of steady business outweigh a one-time higher price, especially with reputation among small traders at stake. It turns on whether enough stock remains after honoring the promise to still profit from the new offer.
turns_on: whether enough stock remains to satisfy both buyers
